Congress Clocks In
The 119th Congress
resumed
yesterday for the first time since last week’s wave of Democratic victories (
see latest
). Republicans have five scheduled legislative weeks left before losing control of both houses in January.
Chief among Republican priorities is to pass a funding bill ahead of a Dec. 11 government shutdown deadline. Garnering support for the Pentagon’s annual policy bill amid an
unpopular Iran war
is also a priority. It also comes as outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R, KY-4)
reintroduced a resolution
yesterday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on eight counts, including over his handling of the Iran war; a House vote could come as soon as this week. Massie separately predicts he will amass the 218 signatures necessary to force floor action on the Justice Department’s handling of the
Epstein files

COP31 Begins
The United Nations’
annual climate summit
, known as the Conference of the Parties or COP, kicked off its 31st gathering yesterday in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators from nearly 200 countries will participate in the event; the US did not send an official federal delegation for the second consecutive year.
COP31 commenced days after a European climate monitoring service reported that last month was the
warmest October
ever recorded. It also marked the third straight month to exceed the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold. Over the next two weeks, delegates will push countries to honor their previous emissions-reduction pledges and work to provide developing nations with funds to adapt to a warming climate. They will also try to resolve deadlocks over how to transition away from fossil fuels.
Those efforts come as a recent UN report found the US
drove one-third of the rise in global emissions
last year, outpacing every other major economy. See an interactive visualization of greenhouse gas emissions worldwide

School Closures Surge
A total of 1,156 US public schools closed during the last academic year, the highest number since the pandemic. The figure, from a
new analysis
published this week, largely reflects declining birth rates and funding cuts.
Student enrollment is falling faster than public schools are closing, with enrollment down by roughly 1.4 million students from 2019 to 2024. Analysts say the decline is primarily due to a multidecade
drop in birth rates
; the under-18 population fell by roughly 2.1 million children from 2010 to 2025. The federal immigration crackdown and postpandemic expansion of private school vouchers and homeschool options have also contributed. Projections indicate that tumbling enrollment could cost public schools roughly $11.5B in state funding annually by 2030-31, compared with revenue received in 2025-26, potentially spurring further closures.
Research
shows
closures may not deliver the savings school districts expect, since busing, severance, and vacant-building security add costs. Displaced students also often experience long-term declines in reading and math scores. Compare state test scores
